e-5504.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
e-5504.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which $\lambda_1=-1,$ $\lambda_2=1,$ $\lambda_3=0$ are eigenvalues, and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/28c1e8d1a466398336c357726d7f345a39e6ace73ab4b36147328b3f0a7313b9.png)
are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/5611ead246c3e5a26d991603a68f3326b1c381d44eddd116316ca7ea6427fdd8.png)
e-5504.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are $\lambda_1={\color{blue}-1},$ $\lambda_2={\color{red}1},$ $\lambda_3=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/65491fb3de59e45bffb4774aca31cc25f20f555f18ffafc8d56221c689520380.png)

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1={\color{blue}-1},$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2={\color{red}1},$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_3=0.$

Therefore, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/3798d5e0b3305070161e2df70796a20a8fcd1e11f11cecdc94d59db520582ca3.png)

Finally, we obtain

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/1448624dbf0dbb227d5e2a3f082dbda389c521d905b1eee1aafe9a2226e25cfd.png)

In conclusion, we get $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-1.$

e-5505.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
e-5505.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/62f202b2fdbe406e4785cc4acf7f2b9aaa09980bc894340716fbbe5600fb8ae9.png)
Determine whether $A=PDP^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
e-5505.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 6 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )([{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2]-12) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(\lambda -5)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=4,$ $\lambda_2=5,$ and $\lambda_3=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/2f943468de2124874c2d806db25c6ca91a2df9a74902af95220e4974e5ef483b.png)

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible  diagonal matrix is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/6f73d40195a91530d761d966db886e9ad2d87d7fc1059a4112a0a2701ce6a72f.png)

e-5506.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
e-5506.problem:
Consider the following matrices:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/7d992806d0d5b90b65030f8c0080f105f67fbb7b4d3d807c3a719307e0c31e40.png)
Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the first column of the matrix $P.$
e-5506.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are  

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=-2, \quad$ $\lambda_2=-1, \quad$ $\lambda_3=2.$ 

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_1=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & 6 \\ -9 & -7 & 9 \\ -16 & -10 & 14\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 \\ -9 & -5 & 9 \\ -16 & -10 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ -9 & -5 & 9 & 0 \\ -16 & -10 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{8}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3} & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get $x_1=x_3.$
Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/fdf2311a1010ed8e8f25623328171687a63ea5da80f6e18a1a8dfbff9e5fae42.png)

Therefore, setting $x_3=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/34e8934a56885ec189cc1819b1336f5b52b7708a092233e3c20e0960218cad10.png)

Finally, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/ec378af1062dda61e89d060d565ef70bf7593a723bd3cba78dfd86f0d027dc5d.png)

e-7330.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/ca47231d1f55afd5641f3924cae2252af74467ba29adbbdb51832cbd4cf06663.png) 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=2,$ $\lambda_2=1,$ and $\lambda_3=0.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
e-7330.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=2,\quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ $\lambda_3=0.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For $\lambda_1=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/b88fd696293e4151a71ca12d25cb56821ba034e07a876777fa30d5d6f6b9c4c3.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/38941ad5615365437a1aee93f085b33d6a240c5a61ce8e0f0a10acb465de0f18.png)

- For $\lambda_3=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/a3ea884b0f6ba11582eb72e6cffcc871a144e55c446aaa304e1c7f9face13c7b.png)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/cc87c4f07116bf301d115ffeb00e81f9cd25d21cb40f61fdbc310f86557a61b4.png)

before.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=2, λ2=−3, λ3=1 are eigenvalues, and v1=[101],v2=[220],v3=[111] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[200030001] and P=[121011101]
b
D=[2000−30001] and P=[121021101]
c
D=[2000−30001] and P=[121001100]
d
D=[2000−30001] and P=[12−1120−101]
e
D=[0010−30200] and P=[121120101]
Submit

decision.explanation: Place the eigenvalues 2, -3, 1 on D's diagonal and the corresponding eigenvectors as columns of P. This gives option b. Since the eigenvalues are distinct, these eigenvectors are linearly independent, so P is invertible; AP=PD implies A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=2, λ2=−3, λ3=1 are eigenvalues, and v1=[101],v2=[220],v3=[111] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[200030001] and P=[121011101]
b
D=[2000−30001] and P=[121021101]
c
D=[2000−30001] and P=[121001100]
d
D=[2000−30001] and P=[12−1120−101]
e
D=[0010−30200] and P=[121120101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=2, λ2=−3, λ3=1, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[2000−30001].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=2,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−3, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=1.

Therefore, we get

P=[121021101].

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=1, λ2=2, λ3=3 are eigenvalues, and v1=[021],v2=[210],v3=[−102] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[100020003] and P=[02−1220101]
b
D=[200010003] and P=[02−1201102]
c
D=[300010002] and P=[00−1210122]
d
D=[100020003] and P=[02−1210102]
e
D=[300020001] and P=[02−1110202]
Submit

decision.explanation: Construct P with columns v₁, v₂, v₃ and D with matching diagonal entries 1, 2, 3. These are exactly the matrices in option d. The distinct eigenvalues ensure P is invertible, and AP=PD gives A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=1, λ2=2, λ3=3 are eigenvalues, and v1=[021],v2=[210],v3=[−102] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[100020003] and P=[02−1220101]
b
D=[200010003] and P=[02−1201102]
c
D=[300010002] and P=[00−1210122]
d
D=[100020003] and P=[02−1210102]
e
D=[300020001] and P=[02−1110202]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=1, λ2=2, λ3=3, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[100020003].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=1,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=2, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=3.

Therefore, we get

P=[02−1210102].

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: D has diagonal entries 1, 2, 3, and P has the corresponding eigenvectors as columns. Thus AP=PD and, since P is invertible, A=PDP^{-1}. The displayed incorrect result concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=−3, λ2=4, λ3=5 are eigenvalues, and v1=[530],v2=[3−12],v3=[−13−1] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[−300040005] and P=[53−13−1302−1]
b
D=[−300010005] and P=[1303−1300−1]
c
D=[−5000−40003] and P=[53−13120−1−1]
d
D=[−300040005] and P=[−33−1313024]
e
D=[−300010005] and P=[53−13−1202−1]
Submit

decision.explanation: Place the eigenvalues -3, 4, 5 on D's diagonal and the corresponding eigenvectors as columns of P. This gives option a. The distinct eigenvalues ensure P is invertible, and AP=PD implies A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].

content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 13\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=13,$ and $c=3.$

Question 4

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=−4, λ2=3, λ3=0 are eigenvalues, and v1=[−121],v2=[−2−32],v3=[1213] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[−1−21a−3212b][−4000c0000][−1−21a−3212b]−1?

a
a=−2, b=13, and c=3
b
a=2, b=−3, and c=0
c
a=−1, b=−4, and c=3
d
a=2, b=13, and c=3
e
a=2, b=3, and c=13
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−4, λ2=3, λ3=0, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−400030000].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−4,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=3, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=0.

Therefore, we get

P=[−1−212−321213].

Finally, we obtain

A=[−1−212−321213][−400030000][−1−212−321213]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=2, b=13, and c=3.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms a=2 and b=13 by placing the eigenvectors in P's columns, and c=3 from the corresponding second eigenvalue. This matches option d. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option c.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 13\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=13,$ and $c=3.$

a

b

decision.explanation: The columns of P must be the corresponding eigenvectors: the first gives a=2, and the second gives b=1. The second diagonal entry is the eigenvalue -2, so c=-2. These values match option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & b & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & b & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-2.$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=1, λ2=−2, λ3=2 are eigenvalues, and v1=[2−11],v2=[011],v3=[10−1] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[a01−1101b−1][1000c0002][a01−1101b−1]−1?

a
a=1, b=1, and c=2
b
a=2, b=−2, and c=1
c
a=1, b=2, and c=−2
d
a=−2, b=1, and c=2
e
a=2, b=1, and c=−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=1, λ2=−2, λ3=2, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[1000−20002].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=1,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=−2.

Therefore, we get

P=[201−11011−1].

Finally, we obtain

A=[201−11011−1][1000−20002][201−11011−1]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=2, b=1, and c=−2.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & b & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & b & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-2.$

before.name: Question 6
before.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$

Question 6
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[2−400−20−66−4]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−400020002]
b
D=[40002000−2]
c
D=[−40001000−2]
d
D=[−40002000−2]
e
D=[−400020004]
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is det(A−λI)=(−4−λ)(2−λ)(−2−λ), so the eigenvalues are −4, 2, and −2. Three distinct real eigenvalues guarantee diagonalizability over the reals. Thus option d gives a valid D; other orderings of these eigenvalues also work with correspondingly ordered eigenvectors.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[2−400−20−66−4]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−400020002]
b
D=[40002000−2]
c
D=[−40001000−2]
d
D=[−40002000−2]
e
D=[−400020004]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|2−λ−400−2−λ0−66−4−λ|=0(−4−λ)|2−λ−40−2−λ|=0(−4−λ)(2−λ)(−2−λ)=0

Therefore, the eigenvalues of A are λ1=−4, λ2=2, and λ3=−2. Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, A is diagonalizable.

We construct a diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix D is D=[−40002000−2]

Note that the diagonal matrix D is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

[−4000−20002].

verification.explanation: Rechecking gives det(A−λI)=(−4−λ)(2−λ)(−2−λ). The three distinct real eigenvalues −4, 2, and −2 guarantee real diagonalizability, so option d is valid and matches the worked solution. Permuting these diagonal entries also works with corresponding columns of P permuted. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[114050111]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−10003000−5]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[5000−10003]
d
D=[100020003]
e
D=[50001000−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: Expanding along the second row gives det(A−λI)=(5−λ)((1−λ)^2−4)=(5−λ)(λ+1)(λ−3). The eigenvalues 5, −1, and 3 are distinct and real, so A is diagonalizable over the reals. Option c is a valid D; other orderings also work with matching eigenvector columns in P.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable.  

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.html:
Question 7
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[114050111]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−10003000−5]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[5000−10003]
d
D=[100020003]
e
D=[50001000−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|1−λ1405−λ0111−λ|=0(5−λ)|1−λ411−λ|=0(5−λ)((1−λ)(1−λ)−4)=0(5−λ)(λ2−2λ−3)=0(5−λ)(λ+1)(λ−3)=0.

Therefore, the eigenvalues of A are λ1=5,λ2=−1 and λ3=3. Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, A is diagonalizable.

We construct a diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix D is

D=[5000−10003].

Note that the diagonal matrix D is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

[3000−10005].

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable.  

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: Expanding along the second column gives det(A−λI)=(4−λ)(λ²+3λ+11). The quadratic has discriminant 9−44=−35, so two eigenvalues are nonreal. Therefore A cannot be diagonalized with real P and real D, which is the meaning of option c in this question.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 \\ 6 & 4 & 9 \\ -7 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & 3 \\ 6 & 4-\lambda  & 9 \\ -7 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -7 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+21) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +11) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial ${\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +11=0,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[203649−70−5] Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−100040003]
b
D=[−100060004]
c
A is not diagonalizable
d
D=[4000−10008]
e
D=[−200040003]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|2−λ0364−λ9−70−5−λ|=0(4−λ)|2−λ3−7−5−λ|=0(4−λ)((2−λ)(−5−λ)+21)=0(4−λ)(λ2+3λ+11)=0

For the quadratic polynomial λ2+3λ+11=0, we have that the discriminant D<0. So, it doesn't have real roots.

Therefore, A is not diagonalizable over R.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms det(A−λI)=(4−λ)(λ²+3λ+11). The quadratic has discriminant −35, so A has nonreal eigenvalues and cannot be diagonalized over the reals. Thus option c satisfies the stated real-matrix requirement. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 \\ 6 & 4 & 9 \\ -7 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & 3 \\ 6 & 4-\lambda  & 9 \\ -7 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -7 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+21) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +11) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial ${\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +11=0,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[1−200−10−33−2]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−20001000−1]
b
D=[20001000−1]
c
D=[−20002000−1]
d
D=[20001000−2]
e
D=[−200010001]
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is det(A−λI)=(−2−λ)(1−λ)(−1−λ). Its three distinct real eigenvalues are −2, 1, and −1, so A is diagonalizable over the reals. Option a gives a valid D; permuting these entries also works with correspondingly ordered eigenvectors in P.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )(-1-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[1−200−10−33−2]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[−20001000−1]
b
D=[20001000−1]
c
D=[−20002000−1]
d
D=[20001000−2]
e
D=[−200010001]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|1−λ−200−1−λ0−33−2−λ|=0(−2−λ)|1−λ−20−1−λ|=0(−2−λ)(1−λ)(−1−λ)=0

Therefore, the eigenvalues of A are λ1=−2, λ2=1, and λ3=−1. Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, A is diagonalizable.

We construct a diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix D is D=[−20001000−1]

Note that the diagonal matrix D is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

[−2000−10001].

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )(-1-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[20−6143130−5]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
A is not diagonalizable
b
D=[300040000]
c
D=[300030003]
d
D=[20003000−5]
e
D=[−100040003]
Submit

decision.explanation: Expanding along the second column gives det(A−λI)=(3−λ)((2−λ)(−5−λ)+18)=(3−λ)(λ²+3λ+8). The quadratic has discriminant 9−32=−23, so two eigenvalues are nonreal. Therefore A is not diagonalizable over the reals, as required by the question; option a applies.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -6 \\ 3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+18) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial  $\,{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8\,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

Question 10
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[20−6143130−5]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
A is not diagonalizable
b
D=[300040000]
c
D=[300030003]
d
D=[20003000−5]
e
D=[−100040003]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|2−λ0−6143−λ130−5−λ|=0(3−λ)|2−λ−63−5−λ|=0(3−λ)((2−λ)(−5−λ)+18)=0(3−λ)(λ2+3λ+8)=0

For the quadratic polynomial λ2+3λ+8 we have that the discriminant D<0. So, it doesn't have real roots.

Therefore, A is not diagonalizable over R.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given Matrix Is Diagonalizable Over the Real Numbers
content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -6 \\ 3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+18) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial  $\,{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8\,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & ∗ \\ 1 & 0 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]

b

decision.explanation: Using the explicitly corrected P, choose v=(−2,1,2). Then Av=(2,−1,−2)=−v. The corrected first two columns satisfy A(1,0,0)=3(1,0,0) and A(1,1,0)=5(1,1,0), so AP=PD. Also det(P)=2, ensuring P is invertible. Thus option b satisfies the corrected request; any nonzero scalar multiple of v also works.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & ∗ \\ 1 & 0 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2(\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3})-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Question 11
?

Consider the following matrices: A=[32305−300−1],D=[30005000−1],P=[11∗10∗00∗] Given that D=P−1AP, find the third column of the matrix P.

a
[−2−14]
b
[−212]
c
[−1−12]
d
[−1−21]
e
[2−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of A are

λ1=3, λ2=5, λ3=−1.

So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=−1. Computing A−(−4)I, we get

A−λ3I=[32305−300−1]−(−1)[100010001]=[42306−3000].

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix M is M=[423006−300000].

The above matrix is already in row echelon form. It has two pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=12x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we get x1=14(−2(12x3)−3x3)=14(−4x3)=−x3. Hence, the general solution is [−x312x3x3],x3∈R. Therefore, setting x3=2, we get the eigenvector

v3=[−212].

Finally, P=[1−1−201−100−2].

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & ∗ \\ 1 & 0 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2(\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3})-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

decision.explanation: The first column must have eigenvalue −1. For v=(1,1,1), Av=(−1,−1,−1)=−v. The supplied second and third columns have eigenvalues 1 and 3, respectively, so AP=PD. These eigenvectors have distinct eigenvalues and are linearly independent, ensuring P is invertible. Thus option d works; any nonzero scalar multiple of v also works.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 & 1 \\ ∗ & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the first column of the matrix $P.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 12

Consider the following matrices: A=[5−4−20−104−4−1],D=[−100010003],P=[∗11∗00∗21] Given that D=P−1AP, find the first column of the matrix P.

a
[−211]
b
[2−12]
c
[011]
d
[111]
e
[434]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of A are

λ1=−1, λ2=1, λ3=3.

So, the first column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get

A−(−1)I=[5−4−20−104−4−1]−(−1)[100010001]=[6−4−20004−40].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[6−4−2000004−400]R1:=12R1R3:=14R3∼[3−2−1000001−100]R2↔R3∼[3−2−101−1000000]R2:=R2+(−13)R1∼[3−2−100−131300000]

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 & 1 \\ ∗ & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the first column of the matrix $P.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Consider the following matrices: A=[15−4−1640−5−40−1019],D=[15000−10005],P=[1∗04∗−4−1∗1]

Given that A=PDP−1, find the second column of the matrix P.

a
[40−4]
b
[−4−51]
c
[101]
d
[0−10]
e
[−111]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of A are

λ1=15, λ2=−1, λ3=5.

So, the second column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ2=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−1. Then A−λ2I=[15−4−1640−5−40−1019]−(−1)[100010001]=[16−4−1640−4−40−10110].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[16−4−16040−4−400−101100]R1:=−116R1R3:=R3+14R2∼[1−14−1040−4−4000000]R2:=R2−40R1∼[1−14−1006000000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we get x1=x3. Hence, the general solution is

[x30x3],x3∈R. Therefore, setting x3=1, we get the eigenvector

v2=[101].

Finally, P=[11040−4−111].

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}15 & -4 & -16 \\ 40 & -5 & -40 \\ -10 & 1 & 9\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}15 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ & 0 \\ 4 & ∗ & -4 \\ -1 & ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of  the matrix $P.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=15,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get
Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}15 & -4 & -16 \\ 40 & -5 & -40 \\ -10 & 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -4 & -16 \\ 40 & -4 & -40 \\ -10 & 1 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -4 & -16 & 0 \\ 40 & -4 & -40 & 0 \\ -10 & 1 & 10 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{16}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{4} & -1 & 0 \\ 40 & -4 & -40 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-40{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{4} & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & 9 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & a \\ 1 & 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $a+2b.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=8,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=9,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=10.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=10.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=10.$ Computing $A-10I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & 9 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & -1 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & -1 & -3 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-8 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -8 & -1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-8 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3}.$ 
Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=4,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+2b=-4+2(4)=4.$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a & 1 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Computing $A-(-3)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{1}=1.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Computing $A-(-3)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{1}=1.$

a
D=[−6000−7000−9] and P=[−1−12−201021]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[600070009] and P=[−1−1−2−212201]
d
D=[600070009] and P=[−1−12−201021]
e
D=[−6000−7000−9] and P=[−1−1−2−212201]
Submit

decision.explanation: In option c, the columns of P are v₁=(−1,−2,2), v₂=(−1,1,0), and v₃=(−2,2,1). Direct multiplication gives Av₁=6v₁, Av₂=7v₂, and Av₃=9v₃, so AP=PD. These nonzero eigenvectors have distinct eigenvalues, hence P is invertible and D=P^{-1}AP.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 9 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

Question 16
?

A=[4−3−4294229] The matrix A has eigenvalues λ1=6, λ2=7, and λ3=9. Find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[−6000−7000−9] and P=[−1−12−201021]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[600070009] and P=[−1−1−2−212201]
d
D=[600070009] and P=[−1−12−201021]
e
D=[−6000−7000−9] and P=[−1−1−2−212201]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix:

λ1=6, λ2=7, λ3=9.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A. Applying our usual method, we get the following.

  • For λ1=6, we get A−6I=[−2−3−4234223]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v1=[−1−22].

  • For λ2=7, we get A−7I=[−3−3−4224222]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−7I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v2=[−110].

  • For λ3=9, we get A−9I=[−5−3−4204220]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−9I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v3=[−221].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[600070009],P=[−1−1−2−212201]

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 9 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

A=[20−26−1−10001] The matrix A has eigenvalues λ1=1, λ2=−1, and λ3=2. Find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that A=PDP−1.

a
D=[1000−10002] and P=[−1011−121−10]
b
D=[1000−10002] and P=[201112100]
c
D=[1000−10002] and P=[101102−100]
d
D=[1000−10002] and P=[1011−12110]
e
D=[1000−10002] and P=[211122130]
Submit

decision.explanation: Option b has columns v₁=(2,1,1), v₂=(0,1,0), and v₃=(1,2,0). Direct multiplication gives Av₁=v₁, Av₂=−v₂, and Av₃=2v₃, so AP=PD. The distinct eigenvalues ensure these eigenvectors are linearly independent and P is invertible. Therefore A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -1 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -3 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix:

λ1=1, λ2=−1, λ3=2.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A. Applying our usual method, we find the following.

  • For λ1=1, we get A−I=[10−26−2−10000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v1=[211].

  • For λ2=−1, we get A−(−1)I=[30−260−10002]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v2=[010].

  • For λ3=2, we get A−2I=[00−26−3−1000−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v3=[120].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[1000−10002],P=[201112100]
