Thus AP=PD, and the distinct eigenvalues ensure P is invertible, giving A=PDP^{-1}. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -1 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -3 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 18
?

A=[2−3001001−1] The matrix A has eigenvalues λ1=2, λ2=−1, and λ3=1. Find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that A=PDP−1.

a
D=[2000−10001] and P=[610002011]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[2000−10001] and P=[116−102011]
d
D=[2000−10001] and P=[102006011]
e
D=[2000−10001] and P=[106002011]
Submit

decision.explanation: Option e has columns (1,0,0), (0,0,1), and (6,2,1). Multiplying by A gives respectively 2(1,0,0), −(0,0,1), and (6,2,1), so AP=PD. These eigenvectors have distinct eigenvalues, ensuring P is invertible and A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 18
?

A=[2−3001001−1] The matrix A has eigenvalues λ1=2, λ2=−1, and λ3=1. Find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that A=PDP−1.

a
D=[2000−10001] and P=[610002011]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[2000−10001] and P=[116−102011]
d
D=[2000−10001] and P=[102006011]
e
D=[2000−10001] and P=[106002011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix:

λ1=2, λ2=−1, λ3=1.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A. Applying our usual method, we find the following.

  • For λ1=2, we get A−2I=[0−300−1001−3]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives us the eigenverctor v1=[100].

  • For λ2=−1, we get A−(−1)I=[3−30020010]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives us the eigenverctor v2=[001].

  • For λ3=1, we get A−I=[1−3000001−2]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives us the eigenverctor v3=[621].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[2000−10001],P=[106002011]

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

a
D=[−2000−10001] and P=[−101−1421−15]
b
A is not diagonalizable
c
D=[−2000−10001] and P=[011−102121]
d
D=[−2000−10001] and P=[−211−105101]
e
D=[−2000−10001] and P=[11100−210−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: Option c has columns v₁=(0,−1,1), v₂=(1,0,2), and v₃=(1,2,1). Direct multiplication gives Av₁=−2v₁, Av₂=−v₂, and Av₃=v₃, so AP=PD. These nonzero eigenvectors have distinct eigenvalues, making P invertible. Therefore A=PDP^{-1}.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 6 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 6 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 2 \\ -12 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: Option b has columns v₁=(1,1,0), v₂=(−1,1,0), and v₃=(−1,−1,3). Direct multiplication gives Bv₁=5v₁, Bv₂=−3v₂, and Bv₃=2v₃, so BP=PD. Their distinct eigenvalues ensure P is invertible, giving D=P^{-1}BP.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $B$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}BP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-3)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

content.problem:
$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $B$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}BP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-3)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
